title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Poured into AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
dek: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: Explaining US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets on the same funding chain offers a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors tracking both US AI and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary market practitioners judging the source and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The discussion of specific Hong Kong IPO cases can be skipped; the main thread resumes at 8:11 with the Nvidia liquidity experiment.

points.h: Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
points.body: Don't take the low IPO break rate in Hong Kong as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the roughly 50-50 normal level under a market-driven mechanism, meaning the participants were mostly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their IPO prices, indicating that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the root problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI investment, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any major internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the most FOMO quarter across the entire supply chain; everyone rushed to spend money before prices rose, and inventories could still support gross margins. By Q3, inventories are depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so the negative factors will appear together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco launched 'rent-to-own' to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing rent-to-own. In its earnings, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—this is speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from rent-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial measures to maintain capital market expectations, which is similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund raises. The money that will be deployed aggressively in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of CXMT and YMTC, two large language models, and two large chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the state's playbook. So this is not a rational long-term increment but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New property policy removes households from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent property policy is not to rescue developers but to detach households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing objects in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the apartment later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization; buyers now get completed homes and only play the consumer role, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, aiming to stabilize the denominator of the asset side first, avoiding panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

points.h: Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull doesn't rely on shouting; it relies on layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, serving a quasi-stabilizing function; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short—not allowing short-term money from households to be invested in ten-year illiquid assets.

points.h: Crises grow with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises with money printing, and each action is faster. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but it was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so another larger wave of easing was piled on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have at least one and a half bubbles accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face some form of long-term stagflation.

quotes.text: The reason I say it's a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a liquidity peaking problem.
The capital market still thinks whoever spends aggressively is great, but when half-year reports come out, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where, in a sense, it needs to use rent-to-own to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone sees that you can pull off this story once, so they think they can definitely pull it off too—that's roughly the psychology.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently slow and bullish; it needs to first build a chip structure on the basis of a slow bull.
Before the last pile of bubbles had dissipated, an even bigger one was added on top, and it was added without hesitation.
